generates TypeScript definitions for your application's routes without performing a full build. This is useful for IDE autocomplete and CI type-checking of route usage.
Previously, route types were only generated during
directly wouldn't validate your route types. Now you can generate types independently and validate them externally:

# Generate route types first, then validate with TypeScript
next typegen && tsc --noEmit

# Or in CI workflows for type checking without building
next typegen && npm run type-check

analyzes your application's bundle output using
. This command helps you understand the size and composition of your bundles, including JavaScript, CSS, and other assets. This command doesn't produce an application build.
By default, the command starts a local server after analysis completes, allowing you to explore your bundle composition in the browser. The analyzer lets you:
Filter bundles by route and switch between client and server views
View the full import chain showing why a module is included
Trace imports across server-to-client component boundaries and dynamic imports
To write the analysis output to disk without starting the server, use
. Snapshot and interactive UI files are written to

# Build and save a snapshot without starting the UI server
npx next analyze --output --snapshot audit-1

# Stream that saved graph as one JSON object per line, without rebuilding
npx next analyze export --snapshot audit-1 > graph.jsonl

You can build only specific routes in the App and Pages Routers using the
option. This is useful for faster debugging when working with large applications. The
option accepts comma-separated file paths, supports glob patterns, and excludes any path prefixed with

# Build a specific route
next build --debug-build-paths="app/page.tsx"

# Build more than one route
next build --debug-build-paths="app/page.tsx,pages/index.tsx"

# Include route group folders in the path
next build --debug-build-paths="app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx"

# Use glob patterns
next build --debug-build-paths="app/**/page.tsx"
next build --debug-build-paths="pages/*.tsx"

# Exclude routes with a ! prefix
next build --debug-build-paths="app/**/page.tsx,!app/admin/**"

Configuring a timeout for downstream proxies
When deploying Next.js behind a downstream proxy (e.g. a load-balancer like AWS ELB/ALB), it's important to configure Next's underlying HTTP server with

than the downstream proxy's timeouts. Otherwise, once a keep-alive timeout is reached for a given TCP connection, Node.js will immediately terminate that connection without notifying the downstream proxy. This results in a proxy error whenever it attempts to reuse a connection that Node.js has already terminated.
To configure the timeout values for the production Next.js server, pass

NODE_OPTIONS='--throw-deprecation' next
NODE_OPTIONS='-r esm' next
NODE_OPTIONS='--inspect' next
You can capture CPU profiles to analyze performance bottlenecks in your Next.js application. The
flag enables V8's built-in CPU profiler and saves profiles to

# Profile the build process
next build --experimental-cpu-prof

# Profile the dev server (profile saved on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM)
next dev --experimental-cpu-prof

# Profile the production server
next start --experimental-cpu-prof
files can be opened in Chrome DevTools (Performance tab → Load profile) or other V8-compatible profiling tools.
: Profile files are named with a descriptive prefix and timestamp. The profiles generated depend on the command:
- Child server process (request handling and rendering) - this is typically what you want to analyze
